summary: A proposal that an FTP server should allow a limited kind of access without a user name and password, since people were using the mail file facility as a workaround for files they could not otherwise fetch. It suggests a new class of everyone, whether or not logged on. Later notes such as RFC 501 criticized the details.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 487 proposes letting an FTP server transfer files marked as accessible to anyone without requiring a password. It describes the idea as an experiment and notes that BBN TENEX planned an implementation.

subtitle: A proposal for allowing FTP access to files marked as available to everyone.

tldr.problem: FTP servers often required a user name and password even when a person wanted a file without having an account on that host.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal asks a server to check a file's access settings when a request has no user name or password, and allow transfer if the file is marked accessible to anyone.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says BBN TENEX agreed to modify its FTP server and urges other systems to try the service experimentally.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 487's status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC presents an experimental proposal and says BBN TENEX agreed to modify its server.

sections.title: Why FTP Access Was a Problem
sections.content:
Bob Bressler says users had difficulty transferring files from systems with security controls when they did not have access privileges. FTP servers required a user name and password before granting system access, so a person without an account could not request an otherwise accessible file.

The memo says people were using the FTP MAIL FILE facility as a workaround, although that facility was limited and intended for other purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: A server could require a login even when someone only wanted a file available to everyone. The author says users were using the mail feature as a workaround.

sections.title: Access for Everyone
sections.content:
The RFC describes a common file protection model with access for an individual user, a group, or everyone. It proposes defining “everyone” to include people who are not logged in.

Under the proposal, a request without a user name and password causes the FTP server to examine the file's access parameters. If those parameters say the file is accessible to anyone, the transfer should proceed. The memo says the scheme need not grant file-creation privileges and gives an example of receiving a file by appending to an empty file that has unlimited append access.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the file's access setting rather than requiring an account for every request. The proposal separates permission to retrieve an open file from permission to create files.

sections.title: Accounting and the Suggested Trial
sections.content:
The RFC notes that accounting is harder when a file is retrieved from a general system directory because there is no particular user to charge. It says retrieval involves CPU costs, while storing a file in a user's directory also involves secondary-storage charges.

BBN TENEX agreed to modify its FTP server. A note says the implementation would probably require a user name such as FREE or ANONYMOUS but no password. The author urges other systems to offer the service experimentally and says its success should be judged by user response and how FTP is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal recognizes that a site may need to account for the cost of public retrievals. It asks systems to try the idea and judge it by users' responses and use.
